Anubis. The jackal-headed god of mummification, embalming, and the dead. He was the divine mortician who first mummified Osiris, establishing the funerary arts that allowed eternal life in the afterlife. Depicted in black, the color of mummified flesh and fertile Nile mud, Anubis represented both death and regeneration. He was the god of cemeteries, tombs, and all necropoles throughout Egypt. His watchful jackal form protected the dead from grave robbers and desecration. Associated with the embalming process, priests performing mummification wore Anubis masks and were considered his earthly representatives, carrying out his sacred work. Originally, Anubis was the most important god of the dead before Osiris rose to prominence and took much of his role. But Anubis remained central to Egyptian beliefs about death and the afterlife. He served as a guide and protector of souls in the Duat, the underworld, helping the dead navigate dangers and trials. The Wedjat Eye and protective amulets were often associated with Anubis as he guarded the dead. Black jackals naturally inhabited Egyptian cemeteries, leading to his identification with these scavengers of the dead. When Anubis assisted Isis and Nephthys in preserving and restoring Osiris after Set's murder, he established the funerary process that ensured Osiris's resurrection. This made him a crucial figure in enabling Osiris's eternal kingship in the afterlife. Anubis appears throughout the Book of the Dead as a guide and protector of souls, ensuring safe passage through the underworld. Mummified pharaohs were placed under Anubis's protection for eternity, trusting in his guardianship as they journeyed toward resurrection and eternal life.
